$comment: Lifecycle policy for the OFF-PROJECT OBJECT MIRROR, gs://aglyn-dr-storage-mirror (AGL-2422). NOT APPLIED YET — the bucket does not exist. Zach applies it as step 4 of the runbook in docs/DISASTER_RECOVERY.md gap 6, BEFORE the first sync ever runs. Apply with: gcloud storage buckets update gs://aglyn-dr-storage-mirror --lifecycle-file=cloud/storage-mirror-lifecycle.json --project=aglyn-dr  — read it back with: gcloud storage buckets describe gs://aglyn-dr-storage-mirror --format='value(lifecycle_config)' --project=aglyn-dr. Revert with --clear-lifecycle. --lifecycle-file REPLACES the whole config rather than merging, so this file must always carry every rule the bucket should have.
$why: This bucket is the only copy of gs://aglyn-main.appspot.com (451 objects, ~47 MiB of live customer media plus the adminAudit-archive/ and erasures/ prefixes) and gs://aglyn-main-plugin-artifacts (7 publisher-signed bundles that cannot be rebuilt from our source). The transfer that fills it propagates deletes, so that an erasure reaches the copy — otherwise an erased customer's media lives in the mirror forever, which is a DPA §11 answer nobody wants to give. Propagating deletes is only SAFE because object versioning is on: the run that copies a mistaken deletion into the mirror turns the object noncurrent instead of destroying it, and this rule is what bounds how long the undo lasts. Versioning and this rule are one decision made in two places; neither is correct alone.
$never: NO rule here may omit `isLive: false`. Every rule in this document acts on NONCURRENT versions only. A rule that can match a live object would delete the mirror of an object that still exists in production — the mirror's own data-loss event, arriving on a schedule, in the one bucket whose whole job is to still be there. `age` here is age since the version became noncurrent (`daysSinceNoncurrentTime`), never age since upload: an object uploaded two years ago and deleted yesterday must still be recoverable for the full window. tools/scripts/lib/backup-copies.test.mjs fails the build if either invariant is broken.

$periods.noncurrent versions: 30 days. Long enough to notice — the failure this is bought for is a delete nobody sees at the time, and a week (which is what the source bucket's default soft delete already gives) is not enough for one. Short enough that the mirror is not a second, unbounded copy of data a customer asked to have erased: an erasure reaches the mirror on the next sync, the object goes noncurrent, and 30 days later it is gone. That is the same 'a limited period, after which it will be deleted' the DPA §11 language commits to, and the same shape as the source bucket's own erasures/ backstop.

$oneCondition: `daysSinceNoncurrentTime` is the ONLY condition beside `isLive`, and adding `numNewerVersions` beside it would be a bug that reads like a refinement. Lifecycle conditions are ANDed. A DELETED object leaves exactly one noncurrent version with ZERO newer versions, so `numNewerVersions: 2` never matches it — and a deleted object is precisely the case this bucket exists for and the case the DPA bound applies to. The rule would have expired overwrite history on schedule while retaining every erased customer's media forever, and it would have read as the stricter of the two policies to anyone reviewing it.
